title: The UN & International Organizations
hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.
key_points: Intergovernmental organizations (IGOs) are bodies states create to cooperate on shared problems.
The UN is the broadest, founded after WWII to keep peace and foster cooperation.
IGOs provide forums, set standards, and coordinate action — but rely on member states' consent and resources.
They are not world governments: their power is delegated and limited by sovereignty.
content_html: Sovereign states recognize no authority above them — yet they constantly need to coordinate, on everything from trade and disease to aviation and war. One durable solution is the intergovernmental organization (IGO): a standing body that states create and join to cooperate on shared problems, with its own rules, staff, and meetings. There are many — for health, trade, civil aviation, regional security — but the broadest is the United Nations.
extra_html: The UN was founded in 1945, in the wake of two world wars, with the central aim of helping to maintain international peace and security and to foster cooperation among nations. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as a forum where almost every state in the world is represented, working across peacekeeping, development, human rights, and humanitarian relief. But it is essential to understand what IGOs are not: they are not world governments. Their authority is delegated by the member states that create them and is bounded by those states' sovereignty. They provide forums for negotiation, set common standards, gather information, and coordinate collective action — and in doing so they can make cooperation far easier and more routine than it would otherwise be. Yet they generally cannot compel a sovereign state to act against its will, and they depend on members for funding, troops, and compliance. Their real influence therefore comes less from commanding states than from convening them, shaping expectations, and lowering the cost of working together.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

flashcards.back_html: A body that states create to cooperate on shared problems — like the UN — pooling some coordination while keeping their sovereignty.

flashcards.prompt: Why was the United Nations founded after World War II?

choices.text: To help keep international peace and foster cooperation among states
To act as a world government that overrules states
To replace all national militaries with one army

flashcards.explanation_html: The UN was created to prevent another world war and provide a forum for cooperation, not to govern states from above.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the UN not a 'world government'?

choices.text: Its powers are delegated by, and limited by, sovereign member states
It can pass binding laws over any country at will

flashcards.explanation_html: IGOs depend on members' consent and resources; sovereignty limits how much authority states hand over.
